description: Free-body diagrams, resultant forces, Newton's three laws and weight vs mass.
content_html:
What Is a Force?

A force is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in newtons (N) and they always arise from an interaction between two objects. Every time one object exerts a force on another, the second object exerts an equal force back — forces never exist alone.

Forces can be contact forces (friction, tension, normal contact force, air resistance) or non-contact forces (gravity, magnetism, electrostatic attraction). Both types are vector quantities — they have size and direction.

Key Fact

Newton's third law states that when two objects interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in size, opposite in direction, and the same type of force. These forces act on different objects — they never cancel each other out on the same object.

Weight and the Gravitational Field

Weight is a force — the gravitational pull on an object. It is proportional to mass and is calculated using:

$$W = mg$$

where \(W\) is weight in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(g\) is the gravitational field strength in N/kg. Near Earth's surface, \(g \approx 10\) N/kg.

Mass is a measure of how much matter an object contains. It does not change with location. A student with a mass of 60 kg has that same mass whether on Earth, the Moon or in deep space. Their weight, however, changes with location: on Earth \(W = 60 \times 10 = 600\) N; on the Moon, where \(g \approx 1.6\) N/kg, \(W = 60 \times 1.6 = 96\) N.

Weight is measured using a Newton meter (spring balance). Mass is measured using a balance that compares against known masses — this works even in reduced gravity because both sides are equally affected.

Resultant Force

When several forces act on an object, their combined effect can be described by a single resultant force. If forces act in the same direction, they add together. If they act in opposite directions, the smaller is subtracted from the larger — the resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.

Key Fact

If the resultant force is zero, the object is in equilibrium: it stays still or moves at constant velocity. If the resultant force is non-zero, the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force.

A free body diagram represents all the forces acting on one object. Each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the object, pointing in the direction the force acts. The length of each arrow is proportional to the force's size.

Example: a book resting on a table has two forces — its weight acting downwards and the normal contact force from the table acting upwards. If these are equal in size, the resultant is zero and the book stays still. Newton's insight is that this is no coincidence: the book pushes the table down; the table pushes the book up — a Newton's third law pair.

Newton's Laws in Action

Newton's first law: if the resultant force on an object is zero, its velocity does not change. A moving object at zero resultant force keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction — it does not slow down without a force acting on it. This was a profound insight: before Newton (and Galileo before him), many believed a force was needed simply to keep an object moving.

Newton's second law: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass:

$$F = ma$$

where \(F\) is the resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\). A larger force produces a greater acceleration; a larger mass requires a greater force to produce the same acceleration.

A 900 kg car has a driving force of 3600 N and experiences 900 N of friction. Calculate the acceleration.

Step 1: Resultant force = 3600 − 900 = 2700 N (in the direction of motion)

Step 2: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{2700}{900} = 3\) m/s\(^2\)

Always find the resultant force first before substituting into \(F = ma\).

Inertial mass is formally defined as the ratio \(m = F/a\) — how difficult it is to accelerate an object. A heavy truck has far greater inertia than a bicycle: the same resultant force produces much less acceleration. Newton's discovery that this same quantity governs both resistance to acceleration and gravitational attraction (weight) is one of the great connections in physics — a striking example of creative scientific thinking (IaS3).
exam_tip_html: For Newton's third law questions, always identify the two objects in the interaction and state the force pair explicitly — for example, “the Earth pulls the skydiver down with gravity; the skydiver pulls the Earth up with an equal gravitational force.” The common mistake is confusing Newton's third law pairs (on different objects) with balanced forces (on the same object). For \(F = ma\) calculations, always calculate the resultant force first — many students substitute the driving force without subtracting friction, and lose marks. Free body diagrams should always label the type of force (weight, normal contact, friction) not just the direction.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Forces are vector quantities arising from interactions between pairs of objects. Newton's third law: the two forces in an interaction pair are equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type, and act on different objects.
  • Weight \(W = mg\) depends on gravitational field strength; mass does not change with location. Resultant force determines whether an object accelerates. If resultant force is zero, the object is in equilibrium.
  • \(F = ma\): greater force → greater acceleration; greater mass → smaller acceleration for the same force. Free body diagrams summarise all forces on one object and help find the resultant.

practice_questions.text: State Newton's third law of motion. Give one example of a Newton's third law force pair.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: when two objects interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in size, opposite in direction and the same type / act on different objects.
1 mark: a valid example, e.g. a book pushes down on a table (contact force); the table pushes up on the book with an equal contact force — accept any correct pair identifying the two objects and directions.

practice_questions.text: A cyclist of mass 70 kg, including the bicycle, experiences a driving force of 280 N from pedalling and a resistive force of 80 N from air resistance. Calculate the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
Resultant force = 280 − 80 = 200 N [1 mark for correct resultant]
\(a = F/m = 200/70 = 2.86\) m/s\(^2\) (accept 2.9 m/s\(^2\)) [1 mark for correct answer with unit].

Common error: using 280 N rather than the resultant force.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between mass and weight, using an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states mass is measured in kg and weight in N.
Secure: mass is the amount of matter in an object; it does not change with location, measured in kg. Weight is the gravitational force on an object; it depends on the gravitational field strength at that location, measured in N.
Mastering: as Secure, plus gives a numerical example (e.g. a 50 kg student weighs 500 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) but only 80 N on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg); their mass remains 50 kg).

[1 mark: mass = amount of matter, kg, does not change; 1 mark: weight = gravitational force, N, depends on location; 1 mark: valid numerical example]

practice_questions.text: Draw a labelled free body diagram for a skydiver falling at terminal velocity. Use your diagram to explain why the skydiver is not accelerating.
practice_questions.marks:
Diagram [2 marks]: two arrows from the skydiver — weight downward, labelled W (or weight, or mg); drag/air resistance upward, labelled F_drag (or air resistance); both arrows equal in length.

Explanation [2 marks]: the resultant force is zero because weight equals air resistance; by Newton's first law / Newton's second law with F = 0, acceleration = 0, so the skydiver falls at constant (terminal) velocity.

Emerging: draws arrows but does not label or explain.
Mastering: links explicitly to F = ma with F_resultant = 0 → a = 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Newton's discovery of the universal nature of gravity — that the same force causes objects to fall on Earth and keeps the Moon in orbit — is considered an important example of creative thinking in science.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states Newton connected Earth's gravity to the Moon's orbit.
Secure: before Newton, these were considered unrelated phenomena; Newton's insight (IaS3) was to propose that the same mathematical law — gravity decreasing with distance squared — could explain both falling apples and planetary orbits; this required imagination beyond what the observations alone suggested.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that good scientific ideas go beyond the data and make testable predictions; Newton's law correctly predicted the orbits of other planets and eventually led to the discovery of Neptune through orbital anomalies — demonstrating how a creative model can generate new science.

[1 mark: identifies what Newton connected; 1 mark: explains why it required imagination/creativity; 1 mark: notes the law makes testable predictions; 1 mark: gives a specific consequence (e.g. planetary orbit prediction); 1 mark: links to how models in science develop with evidence (IaS3)]

practice_questions.text:
A crate of mass 120 kg is pushed along a flat surface by a force of 360 N. It moves at constant velocity.
(a) What is the resultant force on the crate?
(b) Calculate the friction force acting on the crate.
(c) If the pushing force increases to 480 N while friction stays the same, calculate the new acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Zero [1 mark] — constant velocity means no acceleration, so resultant force = 0 (Newton's first law).

(b) If resultant = 0, friction = driving force = 360 N [1 mark].

(c) Resultant = 480 − 360 = 120 N [1 mark]
\(a = F/m = 120/120 = 1\) m/s\(^2\) [1 mark for calculation, 1 mark for correct unit].

Emergng: correctly answers (a) only.
Secure: correctly answers all three with working shown.
Mastering: explicitly justifies (a) with Newton's first law and links friction = 360 N to equilibrium argument. [1 mark for clear logical justification in (a)/(b)]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the resultant force on an object moving at constant velocity?
options: A force equal to its weight
A force in the direction of motion

knowledge_checks.q: A student has a mass of 55 kg. What is their weight on Earth? (g = 10 N/kg)
Newton's second law can be written as F = _____, where F is the resultant force.
A diagram showing all forces on a single object as labelled arrows is called a _____ diagram.
Match each force type to an example:
right: Friction between a tyre and road
Gravitational attraction between Earth and Moon
Earth pulls you down; you pull Earth up with equal gravity

flashcard_questions.q: State Newton's first law of motion.
flashcard_questions.a: An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

flashcard_questions.q: Give the equation for Newton's second law.
flashcard_questions.a: F = ma (resultant force in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s²).

flashcard_questions.q: State Newton's third law of motion.
flashcard_questions.a: When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a Newton's third law pair and balanced forces?
flashcard_questions.a: Third law pairs act on different objects; balanced forces act on the same object.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a free body diagram?
flashcard_questions.a: A diagram showing all forces on a single object as labelled arrows.
W = mg (weight in N, mass in kg, gravitational field strength in N/kg).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the gravitational field strength at Earth's surface?

flashcard_questions.a: The state when the resultant force on an object is zero — it is stationary or moving at constant velocity.

flashcard_questions.q: A 50 kg object experiences a resultant force of 200 N. What is its acceleration?
Why does a student have the same mass on the Moon but a different weight?
flashcard_questions.a: Mass is the amount of matter (unchanged); weight depends on gravitational field strength, which is lower on the Moon.

glossary_terms.definition: A push or pull arising from an interaction between two objects, measured in newtons (N).
Forces that act between objects in direct physical contact, such as friction, tension and normal contact force.
Forces that act between objects without physical contact, such as gravity, magnetism and electrostatic attraction.
The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons (N). Weight depends on where the object is located.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. Mass is the same everywhere in the universe.
A device used to measure force by the extension of a calibrated spring, also called a spring balance.
The single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined.
The state of an object when the resultant force on it is zero — it is either stationary or moving at constant velocity.
A diagram showing all forces acting on a single object as labelled arrows, each arrow's length proportional to the force magnitude.
The tendency of an object to resist changes to its motion — defined as the ratio of the resultant force to the acceleration it produces.
